questions.title: Regions of the mouth
questions.question: Regarding the mouth, the correct statement is:

options.A: The mouth proper is the all mouth cavity
options.B: The vestibule is the slit-like space separating the lips from the cheeks
options.C: The mouth is divided into vestibule and mouth proper
options.D: The mouth is divided into three parts

explanations.A: Incorrect. The mouth proper is only the inner of the mouth's two regions, not the whole cavity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The vestibule is the slit-like space between the lips/cheeks on the outside and the teeth/gums on the inside, not a space separating the lips from the cheeks themselves.
explanations.C: Correct. The mouth (oral cavity) is divided into two regions: the vestibule, the slit-like space outside the teeth and gums and inside the lips and cheeks, and the mouth proper, the space inside the teeth and gums that extends back to the oropharyngeal isthmus. This two-part division is the standard description of the mouth's regions taught in gross anatomy. Recognising both named regions, and not collapsing them into one cavity or splitting them into three, is what the question is testing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The mouth is divided into two regions, the vestibule and the mouth proper, not three.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Divide the mouth into its vestibule and mouth-proper regions.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: The mouth is divided into vestibule and mouth proper" (Quiz14&15 Q1).

questions.title: Eruption of the permanent third molar
questions.question: The true fact about the permanent teeth is:

options.A: They consist of: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 3 premolars, and 3 molars
options.B: Eruption of them begins at 8 years of age
options.D: The third permanent molar erupts around 18 years (Wisdom tooth)

explanations.A: Incorrect. Each half-jaw's permanent dentition is 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars, and 3 molars, not 3 premolars.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Eruption of the permanent teeth begins around 6 years of age, not 8, with the first permanent molar typically the earliest to erupt.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The full adult permanent dentition numbers 32 teeth, not 33.
explanations.D: Correct. The third permanent molar, popularly called the wisdom tooth, is the last permanent tooth to erupt, typically around 17 to 21 years of age, well after the rest of the permanent dentition is in place. Its late and often crowded eruption, sometimes impacted against the second molar, is why it is singled out for special mention. This late-eruption timing is the true fact the question is testing among the listed statements about the permanent teeth.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State that the third permanent molar (wisdom tooth) is the last permanent tooth to erupt, around 17-21 years.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: The third permanent molar erupts around 18 years (Wisdom tooth)" (Quiz14&15 Q2).

questions.title: Course of the oesophagus
questions.question: The oesophagus is:

options.A: It descends through the thorax only
options.B: It passes through the esophageal hiatus in the diaphragm at the level of the T12 vertebra
options.D: It extends from the pharynx to the stomach

explanations.A: Incorrect. The oesophagus descends through the neck and abdomen as well as the thorax, not the thorax alone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The oesophageal hiatus in the diaphragm lies at the level of the T10 vertebra, not T12.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The oesophagus is roughly 25 cm long, not 28 cm.
explanations.D: Correct. The oesophagus is the muscular tube that extends from the pharynx, at the level of the cricoid cartilage in the neck, down through the neck, thorax and a short abdominal segment to join the stomach at the cardiac orifice. This pharynx-to-stomach course is the defining description of the oesophagus's extent among the four statements offered. Its course through all three body regions, not the thorax alone, is what distinguishes the correct description from the first distractor.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State that the oesophagus extends from the pharynx to the stomach, crossing the neck, thorax and abdomen.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: It extends from the pharynx to the stomach" (Quiz14&15 Q3).

questions.title: The greater curvature of the stomach
questions.question: Regarding the stomach, the correct statement is:

options.A: It has 2 orifices, 3 borders and 2 surfaces
options.B: The lesser curvature forms the shorter left concave border of the stomach
options.C: The pyloric canal is a wide part of the pylorus
options.D: The greater curvature forms the longer left convex border of the stomach

explanations.A: Incorrect. The stomach has 2 orifices, 2 borders (curvatures) and 2 surfaces, not 3 borders.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It is the greater curvature, not the lesser curvature, that is the longer, left, convex border.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pyloric canal is the narrow part of the pylorus, not a wide part; the pyloric antrum is the wider part.
explanations.D: Correct. The stomach has two borders, called curvatures: the lesser curvature is the shorter, right, concave border, while the greater curvature is the longer, left, convex border that runs from the cardiac notch down and around to the pylorus. This left-sided, convex, longer character is what identifies the greater curvature among the stomach's two borders. Getting this pairing right, greater with left/convex/longer and lesser with right/concave/shorter, is the essential distinction being tested.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify the greater curvature as the stomach's longer, left, convex border.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: The greater curvature forms the longer left convex border of the stomach" (Quiz14&15 Q4).

questions.title: Heterochromatin as the inactive chromosome portion
questions.question: The inactive portions of chrmosome are:

explanations.A: Correct. Heterochromatin is the coiled, condensed and transcriptionally inactive portion of the chromosome, staining more deeply basophilic than the rest of the nucleus because its tightly packed DNA is not being actively read. Its condensed state makes the genes within it inaccessible to the transcription machinery, which is exactly why it is described as inactive. This condensed, inactive character is what distinguishes heterochromatin from its uncoiled, transcriptionally active counterpart.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Euchromatin is the loosely coiled, transcriptionally active portion of the chromosome, the opposite of the inactive portion the question asks about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Chromosome" names the whole structure rather than one of its active or inactive portions.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A chromatid is one of the two identical strands of a replicated chromosome, a structural unit rather than a description of activity state.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify heterochromatin as the condensed, transcriptionally inactive portion of the chromosome.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Heterochromatin" (Quiz16&17 Q1).

questions.title: The chromatin network of the nucleus
questions.question: Nucleus contains a network of subdivisions called:

explanations.A: Correct. The interphase nucleus contains a fine, interwoven network of nuclear material called the chromatin network, made of DNA wound around histone proteins and visible as clumps and threads with basic (basophilic) nuclear stains. It is this same chromatin material that condenses into the visible individual chromosomes once the cell enters mitosis. Naming this interphase network as chromatin, rather than as chromosomes, microtubules or microfilaments, is the point of the question.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Microtubules are cytoplasmic cytoskeletal structures organised by the centrosome, not a nuclear network.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Microfilaments are cytoplasmic actin-based cytoskeletal structures, not a subdivision found inside the nucleus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The centrosome is a cytoplasmic microtubule-organising structure lying near the nucleus, not a network found within it.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name chromatin as the network of nuclear material seen in the interphase nucleus.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Chromatin network" (Quiz16&17 Q3).

questions.title: Component excluded from the nucleus
questions.question: The nucleus containing the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Histones are the basic proteins around which nuclear DNA is wound, a genuine nuclear component.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Heterochromatin is the condensed, inactive portion of nuclear chromatin, a genuine nuclear component.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Nucleosomes, the DNA-wound-around-histone-octamer units, are the basic packaging units of nuclear chromatin, a genuine nuclear component.
explanations.D: Correct. An endosome is a cytoplasmic membrane-bound compartment that sorts material taken in by endocytosis on its way to the lysosome or back to the plasma membrane; it is a cytoplasmic organelle, not a component of the nucleus. Histones, heterochromatin and nucleosomes are all genuine parts of the nucleus's own chromatin, which is what makes endosome the one that does not belong on this list. Recognising the endosome as a cytoplasmic, not nuclear, structure is exactly what this except-question is testing.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish genuine nuclear components (histones, heterochromatin, nucleosomes) from the cytoplasmic endosome.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Endosomes" (Quiz16&17 Q4).

questions.title: The nucleolus and protein formation
questions.question: Protein formation is enabled through:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum synthesises lipids and detoxifies substances; it plays no part in ribosome or protein synthesis, unlike the ribosome-studded rough ER.
explanations.B: Correct. The nucleolus is the site within the nucleus where ribosomal RNA is transcribed and assembled together with proteins into the ribosomal subunits that are then exported to the cytoplasm. Because ribosomes are the machines that translate messenger RNA into protein, the nucleolus's role in producing ribosomal subunits makes it the structure that enables protein formation. This ribosome-manufacturing role is the nucleolus's defining function.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mitosis is nuclear and cell division, a process unrelated to enabling protein synthesis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lysosomes are digestive organelles that break proteins down, the opposite of enabling their formation.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the nucleolus enables protein formation by producing the ribosomal subunits.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Nucleoli" (Quiz16&17 Q5).

questions.title: Chromatin as the protein material of chromosomes
questions.question: Chromosomes are made up of special material of protein called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Adenine is a nitrogenous base within DNA, not the protein-containing material chromosomes are built from.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Thymine is likewise a nitrogenous base within DNA, not a protein-containing chromosomal material.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cytosine is another nitrogenous base within DNA, not the protein-containing chromosomal material.
explanations.D: Correct. Chromosomes are built from chromatin, the complex of DNA wound around histone (basic) proteins that forms the fine network seen in the interphase nucleus and condenses into visible individual chromosomes at mitosis. Calling this material chromatin, rather than naming one of the individual DNA bases, is what distinguishes the correct answer from the three distractors. This same chromatin material is what forms the chromatin network tested elsewhere in this cluster.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name chromatin as the DNA-and-histone-protein material chromosomes are built from.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Chromatin" (Quiz16&17 Q14).

questions.title: The centromere as the site of chromatid fusion
questions.question: Chromatids fusion occurs at the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Telomeres are the specialised caps at each chromosome's two ends, not the site of attachment between its two chromatids.
explanations.B: Correct. The centromere is the constricted region of a replicated chromosome at which its two identical sister chromatids remain joined to each other. It is also the site where the kinetochore assembles and spindle fibres attach during mitosis, which is what lets the centromere pull the two chromatids apart into separate daughter cells once fusion is released. This dual role, holding the chromatids together and then serving as the spindle-attachment point, is what makes the centromere the site of chromatid fusion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A secondary constriction is a narrowing elsewhere on the chromosome, distinct from the primary constriction (centromere) where the chromatids are joined.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Histones are the basic proteins around which DNA is wound, not a site or structure on the chromosome.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify the centromere as the site at which the two sister chromatids of a replicated chromosome remain joined.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Centromeres" (Quiz16&17 Q15).

questions.title: Haploid germ cells versus diploid somatic cells
questions.question: Diploid chromosome number is found in normal body cell whereas haploid is found in:

explanations.A: Correct. Ordinary somatic (body) cells carry the diploid chromosome number, two copies of each chromosome, one inherited from each parent. Mature germ cells, the sperm and the ovum, are the exception: meiosis halves their chromosome number to haploid, a single copy of each chromosome, so that fertilisation restores the diploid number in the resulting zygote. This diploid-to-haploid halving is unique to the germ-cell line and does not occur in any other body cell type.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sensory cells are ordinary somatic cells and carry the diploid chromosome number like any other body cell.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Skin cells are likewise ordinary somatic cells with the diploid chromosome number.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Brain cells are also ordinary somatic cells and carry the diploid chromosome number.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that germ cells alone carry the haploid chromosome number, in contrast to the diploid number of somatic cells.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Germ cells" (Quiz16&17 Q16).

questions.title: Colchicine in karyotyping
questions.question: The drug which is used in karyotyping:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Feulgen is a staining reaction used to demonstrate DNA, not a drug used to prepare chromosomes for karyotyping.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Basic" names a class of stain, not a specific drug used in the karyotyping procedure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Giemsa is the stain applied to the chromosome spread to visualise the banding pattern, not the drug that arrests the cells in metaphase beforehand.
explanations.D: Correct. Colchicine is added to a dividing cell culture to arrest cells in metaphase by preventing spindle-fibre formation, which is the stage of the cell cycle at which chromosomes are most condensed and individually distinguishable. The arrested cells are then swollen, fixed, spread onto a slide and stained (commonly with Giemsa) to produce the metaphase spread from which a karyotype is read. Without this colchicine-induced metaphase arrest there would be no well-spread, condensed chromosomes to photograph and analyse.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that colchicine arrests dividing cells in metaphase to produce the chromosome spread used for karyotyping.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Colchicine" (Quiz16&17 Q18); duplicate-of Quiz16&17 Q17 (p186, "Karyotyping requires one of the following" -> Colchisine), not authored twice.

questions.title: The Barr body as an inactivated X chromosome
questions.question: Barr body is:

options.D: A rod like structure in the cytoplasm

explanations.A: Correct. The Barr body is one X chromosome switched off (inactivated) inside the nucleus of a normal female cell, seen microscopically as a small, densely staining mass of heterochromatin attached to the inner nuclear envelope. Because it represents an inactivated X chromosome, a nucleus shows one fewer Barr body than it has X chromosomes in total, which is the basis for using Barr-body counts to screen for X-chromosome number abnormalities. Its identity as an X chromosome, not a Y chromosome or a nucleolar structure, is exactly what this question tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The Barr body is heterochromatin attached to the nuclear envelope, not chromatin associated with the nucleolus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Barr body represents an inactivated X chromosome, not the Y chromosome, which has no equivalent inactivation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The Barr body lies within the nucleus, attached to the nuclear envelope, not as a structure in the cytoplasm.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify the Barr body as an inactivated X chromosome seen as nuclear heterochromatin.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: One of the x chromosome" (Quiz16&17 Q19).

questions.title: The lung as part of the respiratory portion
questions.question: One of the respiratory portion is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The larynx is part of the upper respiratory (conducting) passages, not the respiratory portion where gas exchange takes place.
explanations.B: Correct. The respiratory system's own organ list places the lung, together with its respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli, as its designated respiratory (gas-exchanging) organ, in contrast to the purely conducting passages such as the nose, pharynx, larynx and trachea that only carry air to and from it. This is the sense in which the lung is grouped as the respiratory-portion organ among the four options listed here. Distinguishing an organ whose job is gas exchange from those whose job is only air conduction is the point of the question.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The trachea is a purely conducting air passage, carrying air but not exchanging gas.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The bronchi and the larger bronchioles are also conducting passages; only the airway's smallest, alveoli-bearing branches take part in gas exchange.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the lung as the respiratory (gas-exchanging) organ from the purely conducting airway passages.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: The lung" (Quiz18 Q1).
field_notes.authorNote: The printed key groups "the lung" as the respiratory-portion organ against three purely conducting passages; taught loosely as organ-level classification rather than the stricter histological respiratory-portion/conducting-portion boundary (respiratory bronchiole onward).

questions.title: The paranasal sinuses
questions.question: The air-filled extensions of the respiratory part of the nasal cavity into the cranial bones are:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The nasal cavities are the paired main airway spaces of the nose, not extensions of that airway into the surrounding bones.
explanations.B: Correct. The paranasal sinuses are air-filled spaces within the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid and maxillary bones that develop as outgrowths, or extensions, of the nasal cavity's own respiratory mucosa into the surrounding cranial and facial bones. Each sinus communicates with the nasal cavity through a small opening (ostium), through which it drains and is ventilated. This bone-penetrating, air-filled extension of the nasal mucosa is exactly what distinguishes the paranasal sinuses from the nasal cavity proper.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The nasal septum is the midline partition dividing the nasal cavity into right and left halves, not an air-filled bony extension.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The olfactory area is the specialised smell-sensing mucosa lining the roof of the nasal cavity, not an extension into the surrounding bones.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the paranasal sinuses as air-filled extensions of the nasal cavity into the cranial bones.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: The paranasal sinuses" (Quiz18 Q2).

questions.title: The hilum of the lung
questions.question: The area on the medial surface of lung at which the structures enter and leave the lung:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The root of the lung is the bundle of structures (bronchus, vessels, nerves) itself as it passes to and from the lung, not the area on the lung's surface where they enter and leave.
explanations.B: Correct. The hilum is the roughly triangular area on the medial (mediastinal) surface of each lung through which the bronchus, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, nerves and lymphatics all enter or leave the lung, collectively forming the root of the lung at that point. Naming the hilum as this specific surface area, rather than the structures that pass through it, is what the question asks for. The hilum's position on the medial surface is also why it faces the mediastinum rather than the chest wall.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The apex is the rounded superior tip of the lung, projecting above the first rib, not the site of entry and exit of structures.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The base is the lung's concave inferior surface resting on the diaphragm, not the site where structures enter and leave.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: Identify the hilum as the area on the lung's medial surface where structures forming its root enter and leave.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: The hilum" (Quiz18 Q3).

questions.title: The right lung is larger than the left
questions.question: One of the differences between right and left lung is:

options.A: The right lung is larger and heavier
options.B: Anterior border of the left lung is straight
options.C: The right lung has only one fissure and 2 lobes
options.D: The left lung is shorter and wider

explanations.A: Correct. The right lung is both larger and heavier than the left lung, because the left side of the thorax gives up volume to accommodate the heart, which projects further into the left hemithorax through the cardiac notch of the left lung. This size and weight difference is one of the standard right-versus-left comparisons taught for the lungs. The right lung's greater volume also correlates with its extra lobe (three lobes against the left's two).
explanations.B: Incorrect. It is the left lung's anterior border that is notched by the cardiac notch, not straight; a straight anterior border instead describes the right lung.
explanations.C: Incorrect. It is the right lung that has two fissures (oblique and horizontal) and three lobes, while the left lung has only one (oblique) fissure and two lobes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The left lung is longer and narrower than the right, not shorter and wider, because the right side is foreshortened by the higher right dome of the diaphragm and the left is narrowed by the heart's projection into it.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State that the right lung is larger and heavier than the left, and relate this to the heart's position and the lobar/fissure differences.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: The right lung is larger and heavier" (Quiz18 Q4).

questions.title: Tracheal bifurcation at the sternal angle
questions.question: Regarding the trachea, the true statement is:

options.A: It begins in the neck as a continuation of the larynx at the level of the fourth cervical vertebra
options.B: At the level of the sternal angle trachea bifurcates into a right and left bronchi
options.C: It is kept patent by about 20 complete rings of hyaline cartilage
options.D: It is an elastic tube about 12 cm long

explanations.A: Incorrect. The trachea begins as a continuation of the larynx at the level of the sixth cervical vertebra, not the fourth.
explanations.B: Correct. The trachea descends through the neck and superior mediastinum and terminates by bifurcating into a right and a left principal (main) bronchus at the level of the sternal angle, which corresponds to the T4/T5 vertebral level and marks the boundary between the superior and inferior mediastinum. This sternal-angle bifurcation is a key surface-anatomy landmark used clinically to locate the tracheal carina. The right principal bronchus arising more vertically than the left is a direct consequence of this bifurcation point.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The trachea is kept patent by about 16 to 20 incomplete (C-shaped) cartilage rings, not complete rings; the rings are deficient posteriorly where the trachealis muscle closes the gap.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The trachea is a fibrocartilaginous, not purely elastic, tube about 10 to 11 cm long, not 12 cm.

questions.subject: resp
questions.learning_objective: State that the trachea bifurcates into the right and left principal bronchi at the level of the sternal angle.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: At the level of the sternal angle trachea bifurcates into a right and left bronchi" (Quiz18 Q5).

questions.title: Centrioles and cell division
questions.question: Cytoplasmic structures involved in cell division are:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lysosomes are digestive organelles and take no part in organising cell division.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ribosomes carry out protein synthesis and take no part in organising cell division.
explanations.C: Correct. Centrioles are paired cylindrical cytoplasmic structures that duplicate before mitosis and migrate to opposite poles of the cell, where each pair organises a centrosome that nucleates the microtubules of the mitotic spindle. It is this spindle that attaches to the chromosomes at their centromeres and pulls the sister chromatids apart into the two daughter cells. This spindle-organising role is what makes the centriole, among the organelles listed, the one directly involved in cell division.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mitochondria supply the cell with ATP but do not themselves organise the spindle apparatus of cell division.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: AUN-PMS-102 > Cytology > Cell Cycle and Cell Renewal
questions.learning_objective: State that centrioles organise the mitotic spindle that carries out cell division.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Centrioles" (Quiz19 Q1).

questions.title: DNA replication during S phase
questions.question: The DNA doubles in a stage of cell cycle called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. G2 is the gap phase after DNA replication, during which the cell prepares for mitosis with its DNA content already doubled.
explanations.B: Incorrect. G1 is the gap phase before DNA replication begins, when the cell's DNA content is still at its unreplicated (diploid) amount.
explanations.C: Correct. S (synthesis) phase is the stage of interphase during which the cell replicates its entire DNA content, doubling it from one copy to two identical sister chromatids per chromosome in preparation for division. This doubling is exactly what the S in "S phase" stands for and is the defining event of that stage of the cell cycle. Chromosome replication is therefore correctly located to S phase, not to G1, G2 or M.
explanations.D: Incorrect. M (mitotic) phase is when the already-doubled chromosomes are segregated into two daughter cells, not when DNA is replicated.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: AUN-PMS-102 > Cytology > Cell Cycle and Cell Renewal
questions.learning_objective: Identify S phase as the stage of the cell cycle during which DNA is replicated (doubled).

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: S" (Quiz19 Q2); duplicate-of Quiz19 Q3 (p195, "Chromosome replication occurs during" -> S-phase), not authored twice.

questions.title: Cell death as irreversible cessation of vital activity
questions.question: The irreversible cessation of vital activities inside the cell:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cell cycle is the recurring sequence of growth and division stages a living cell passes through, not the ending of its vital activity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cell differentiation is the process by which a cell acquires a specialised, mature form and function, not the ending of its vital activity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cell growth is an increase in cell size or number as part of normal living activity, not its ending.
explanations.D: Correct. Cell death is defined as the irreversible cessation of a cell's vital activities, the point past which the cell can no longer be revived or continue any of its normal functions. It can occur by different mechanisms, such as necrosis from injury or the programmed process of apoptosis, but in every case the defining feature is that the loss of function is permanent, not simply a slowed or paused metabolic state. This irreversibility is what separates true cell death from a reversible interruption of cell activity.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.module_subject: AUN-PMS-102 > Cytology > Cell Cycle and Cell Renewal
questions.learning_objective: Define cell death as the irreversible cessation of a cell's vital activities.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Cell death" (Quiz19 Q4).

questions.title: Stem cells and asymmetric division
questions.question: What is the role of stem cells with regard to the function of adult tissues and organs?

options.A: Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that divide asymmetrically, giving rise to one daughter that remains a stem cell and one daughter that will differentiate to replace damaged and worn out cells in the adult tissue or organ.
options.B: Stem cells are differentiated cells that reside under the surface of epithelia, in position to take over the function of the tissue when the overlying cells become damaged or worn out.
options.C: Stem cells are differentiated cells and can, when needed, divide to supply new cells for growth of the tissue.
options.D: Stem cells are postmitotic cells which specialize and differentiate.

explanations.A: Correct. A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell that divides asymmetrically: one of its two daughter cells remains an undifferentiated stem cell, preserving the stem-cell population, while the other daughter goes on to differentiate and replace the damaged or worn-out cells of the adult tissue or organ. This self-renewing, asymmetric pattern of division is what lets a small, stable pool of stem cells continuously supply replacement cells throughout adult life without depleting itself. It is this combination, undifferentiated state plus asymmetric self-renewing division, that defines a stem cell functionally.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A stem cell is by definition undifferentiated, not a differentiated cell waiting beneath the epithelium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A stem cell is undifferentiated; a differentiated cell that can still divide when needed instead describes a progenitor or a stable/labile differentiated cell type, not a stem cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A stem cell is not postmitotic; its defining feature is that it keeps dividing throughout life to renew itself and to supply differentiating progeny.

questions.title: Progenitor cells divide infrequently
questions.question: Except one all the following are characteristics of progenitor cells:

options.A: are daughter cells of stem cells
options.B: have reduced potentiality (committed to a single-cell lineage)
options.D: Cells formed by progenitor cells are terminally differentiated

explanations.A: Incorrect. Progenitor cells genuinely do arise as daughter cells of stem cells, so this is a true characteristic, not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Progenitor cells genuinely do have reduced potentiality, being already committed to a single lineage rather than able to give rise to multiple different cell types, so this is a true characteristic, not the exception.
explanations.C: Correct. Unlike stem cells, which divide relatively rarely so as to preserve the long-term stem-cell pool, progenitor cells divide frequently to rapidly amplify their numbers before their progeny go on to terminally differentiate. "Divide infrequently" is therefore the false statement among the four, since it describes the stem cell's own division pattern rather than the progenitor cell's characteristically rapid, transit-amplifying division. This frequent-division behaviour is exactly what lets a small stem-cell pool ultimately supply large numbers of mature, differentiated cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cells progenitor cells give rise to genuinely are terminally differentiated, so this is a true characteristic, not the exception.
